description: Build a simple CRM without code: ten fields, five stages, a next follow-up date on every open lead and a daily list of who to contact.
h1: How to build a simple CRM without code
answer: A simple CRM is one list of leads with about ten fields, five stages from New to Won or Lost, and a "next follow-up" date on every open lead, plus a view sorted by that date so you know who to contact today.
Build it in a sheet or a no-code app; the part that keeps it alive is getting new leads in from your email and forms without typing them.

body.p: Make Stage and Source dropdowns, not free text, so they sort and count. In Google Sheets that is Insert, Dropdown.

sections.h2: When a sheet stops being enough

body.p: HubSpot suggests a sheet strains past about 100 active leads or 500 records; it sells a CRM, so treat the number as a hint. The better signals are practical: two people editing the same lead, follow-ups slipping because nothing reminds you, and leads arriving faster than you can type them in. That is the point to move to an app that captures leads and reminds you, or a full CRM if you have a sales team.

method.h2: How to build it, step by step

steps.title: Make the list with the fields above
steps.body: In a sheet, one tab, one row per lead. In a no-code app, one table.

steps.title: Add the three views
steps.body: A filter view or sorted tab for Follow up; a board for Pipeline if your tool has one.

steps.title: Bring in what you have
steps.body: Paste last quarter’s leads from email and your notes. Fill Stage and Next follow-up for every open one.

steps.title: Decide how new leads get in
steps.body: Form entries, enquiry emails, referrals. Each needs a route into the list, or the CRM goes stale in a month.

steps.title: Set the follow-up rule
steps.body: Every time you contact a lead, set Last contact to today and Next follow-up to a date. No open lead without a date.

steps.title: Review the pipeline weekly
steps.body: Move dead leads to Lost. A pipeline full of ghosts hides the real ones.

body: Captain builds this CRM from one sentence, with the fields, stages and views above. What a sheet cannot do, its crew does: Closer, an AI agent, reads the last day’s email each weekday at 9:00 and adds new people asking to buy, marks leads Replied when they answer, and drafts follow-ups for your approval; Scout, a browser agent, looks up each new lead’s company and adds a note.

wrong.title: Duplicate leads
wrong.body: The same person entered from a form and an email. Use email as the key and search before adding.

wrong.title: Open leads with no date
wrong.body: They never come up in Follow up, so they are forgotten. Make Next follow-up required for every open stage.

wrong.title: Stages nobody agrees on
wrong.body: "Qualified" means three things to three people. Keep five stages with plain names and write one line on what each means.

wrong.title: It goes stale
wrong.body: Leads arrive by email and never reach the list. Automate capture, or set ten minutes a day to add them.

wrong.title: Two people, one sheet
wrong.body: Edits overwrite each other and there is no history. Move to an app with records and a change log.

faqs.q: Can Google Sheets be a CRM?
faqs.a: Yes, for one person or a small team with a few dozen open leads. Add the fields above, dropdowns for stage and source, and a Follow up view sorted by date.

faqs.q: What columns should a simple CRM have?
faqs.a: Name, email, phone, company, source, stage, deal size, last contact, next follow-up and notes. Add more only when you make a decision with them.

faqs.q: When should I move to a real CRM?
faqs.a: When several people work the same leads, when you need email tracking and sequences, or when follow-ups keep slipping despite the sheet.
